reference.source: The Adult and Pediatric Spine (Rothman-Simeone) / Grainger and Allison's Diagnostic Radiology
clinicalPearls: Modic changes are MRI signal changes in the vertebral endplate and adjacent subchondral marrow that accompany degenerative disc disease, most often in the lower lumbar spine
Type 1 represents oedema and fibrovascular marrow, appearing low on T1 and high on T2, and is the type most strongly associated with active low back pain and can enhance with contrast
Type 2 represents fatty marrow replacement, appearing high on T1 and iso- to slightly hyperintense on T2, and is generally regarded as a more stable, less painful state
Type 3 represents subchondral bony sclerosis, appearing low on both T1 and T2 and corresponding to endplate sclerosis on radiographs
The types are dynamic and can convert into one another over time or coexist as mixed patterns, reflecting an evolving degenerative and reparative process

The key differential for a painful type 1 change is infective spondylodiscitis; disc-space and endplate destruction, high T2 disc signal and paravertebral or epidural collections favour infection, whereas Modic changes spare the disc and lack these features
There is no specific treatment for the changes themselves; management targets the underlying discogenic pain and the changes are one factor among many in surgical decision-making
reference.pathophysiology: Modic changes arise from disruption of the vertebral endplate in the setting of degenerative disc disease. Microfractures and increased permeability of the endplate allow mechanical overload and biochemical exposure of subchondral marrow to disc material, provoking a local inflammatory and reparative response. In the acute type 1 pattern there is oedema, granulation tissue and fibrovascular marrow with an inflammatory infiltrate; over time this may resolve into type 2 fatty marrow replacement or type 3 subchondral sclerosis. Proposed drivers include mechanical stress, an autoimmune reaction to sequestered nucleus pulposus, and a contested hypothesis of low-grade colonisation by anaerobic skin organisms, though the changes are classified as a degenerative endplate and marrow phenomenon rather than an infective process. Associated inflammatory mediators sensitise nociceptive fibres in the endplate and outer disc, linking type 1 changes in particular to low back pain.
additionalDifferentials: Seronegative spondyloarthropathy with Andersson lesions or corner inflammation
Haemangioma or focal fatty marrow of the vertebral body
Calcium pyrophosphate or crystal-related endplate change
additionalInvestigations: MRI including T1, T2 and fat-suppressed sequences to classify the change and assess the disc and marrow
Contrast-enhanced MRI when infection or tumour is a concern
Radiographs to demonstrate disc-space narrowing and endplate sclerosis
Inflammatory markers and blood cultures if spondylodiscitis is suspected
Image-guided biopsy or aspiration where infection or malignancy must be excluded
Provocative discography only in selected cases when confirming a discogenic pain source
redFlags: Fever, night pain, raised inflammatory markers or disc-space destruction suggesting spondylodiscitis
Known malignancy, weight loss or a destructive marrow lesion suggesting metastasis or myeloma
Progressive neurological deficit or cauda equina features
An epidural or paravertebral collection on imaging
reference.prognosis: Modic changes are common incidental findings whose clinical significance is variable; type 1 changes correlate best with low back pain and may fluctuate or convert to the more quiescent type 2, and their presence is only one modest factor in the overall prognosis of degenerative disc disease.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting a painful type 1 change as infective spondylodiscitis, or vice versa, and mismanaging the patient
Attributing all of a patient's back pain to Modic changes when they are a frequent incidental finding
Overlooking a destructive or neoplastic marrow lesion by labelling atypical signal as degenerative
Basing surgical decisions on the endplate changes alone without correlating clinical and other imaging findings
